<h2 class="section">The hike</h2>
```

Drove the seven hours from Dublin in two days, with a sleep in the car somewhere in Sligo and a sunrise over Glencar Lough for moral support. Errigal is the white quartzite cone that haunts every photo of Donegal. From a distance it looks fictional. Up close it is extremely real and extremely loose underfoot.

The first half is bog. The second half is scree. The scree is composed entirely of stones that hate you and your ancestors. Two steps up, one step back, repeat for ninety minutes. It is the leg-day-at-the-gym of Irish mountains, and it bills you for it.

The summit is a knife edge about a metre wide with two small cairns and a piece of rusted wire that has been there since at least the Famine and is doing nothing structural. You stand on it. You look at the world. You take exactly one photo because the wind is trying very hard to remove you from the mountain.

The mountain was actually only the second-best moment of the trip. The first was that night. I drove down to a rough pull-in near the coast, parked up, made dinner on the stove and looked up. The sky was green. Then it was pink. Then it was green again with vertical curtains in it.

The northern lights, in Ireland, in real life, not on Instagram. I stood in a field for the better part of an hour and did not check my phone, did not film a TikTok, did not even take a particularly good photo. I just stood there. It was, in the genuine and not annoying sense of the word, religious.

<h2 class="section">Reflections</h2>
```

Errigal in the wet would be a bad idea bordering on a death sentence. Go on a dry day. If you are unsure, do not go. Bring poles. I did not, again. I ate it twice on the way down on dry rock. Twenty-two years old and already this slow to learn.

Slieve League cliffs are forty-five minutes south by car and worth the detour. Highest accessible sea cliffs in the country. Bring a hat that fits properly.
